Page: Overtonium controls: every knob on a channel strip
URL: https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/controls/
Last changed: 2026-10-15

# Controls

Thirty-two channel strips, a noise channel, and a bar of global controls across the top. Every strip has the same twenty-three controls. That is seven hundred and thirty-six of them before the bar is counted, so much of the design is about not having to move them one at a time.

This page covers the mixer. The bar across the top, from the oscillator character to the output stage, is covered on [Effects](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/effects/). Playing the instrument from a keyboard, a host or a controller is covered on [Playing](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/).

## A channel strip

[Image: A close view of the first six channels, showing the row captions in the gutter with the pointer tool button above them, and the interval colour of each channel.]

Six channels and the caption gutter. Each row is named once on the left instead of on every strip.

| Control | Range | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| TUNE | equal to just | Where this partial sits between the tempered position and the exact ratio. The readout shows the resulting cent offset. On the six octave channels both tunings agree, so the knob has nothing to move and the readout stays at 0.0 |
| PITCH MOD shape, rate, depth | Eight shapes, 0.01 to 30 Hz, 0 to 1200 cents | Per-partial vibrato |
| DRIFT | 0 to 25 cents | Smooth random pitch wander, its own stream per partial |
| GLIDE | Off to 5 s | How long this partial takes to reach a new note, so the partials can arrive one at a time. The L and T switches beside the caption, and the knob's right-click menu, set whether it glides always or only legato, and at a fixed rate or in a fixed time. See [Glide](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#glide) |
| ENVELOPE strike, delay, A, D, S | -100 to +100%, 0 to 5 s, 90° then 0.2 ms to 5 s, 1 ms to 20 s, 0 to 100% | Exponential decay. The harder the key is struck, the sooner and faster STRIKE starts the partial |
| KEY OFF swell, level, release | 0 to 5 s, 0 to 100%, 1 ms to 20 s | A second envelope that runs when the key is released |
| AMP MOD shape, rate, depth | Seven shapes, 0.01 to 30 Hz, 0 to 100% | Per-partial tremolo |
| VELOCITY | -100 to +100% | How much key velocity scales this partial. Negative inverts it |
| AFTERTOUCH | -100 to +100% | How much key pressure moves this partial. Negative fades it out |
| PAN | hard left to hard right | Equal power, so the level stays the same as the partial moves across the stereo field |
| M and S |  | Mute overrides solo. Right-click either one to clear every mute or every solo at once |
| LEVEL | -inf to 0 dB | Fader scaled in decibels, with the meter inside its track |

## What the modulators trace

Both per-partial modulators have a shape as well as a rate and a depth. You pick the shape from a small drawing of the wave between the two knobs. Click it to see the list by name. Pitch has eight shapes and amplitude has seven. Each channel has its own, the noise channel included, so the fifth partial can switch on and off while the fourth swells smoothly.

| Shape | What it does |
|---|---|
| Sine | The default |
| Triangle | The same range at an even speed, which sounds more mechanical than a sine |
| Sawtooth, Reverse Sawtooth | A ramp and a sudden jump back, in either direction |
| Square | Two values and nothing in between. On pitch it is a trill. It comes in a bipolar form, which goes the same distance above and below the note, and a unipolar form, which only goes up |
| Sample & Hold | A new random value each cycle, held until the next. On pitch, with the depth at full, it plays random notes anywhere within an octave above or below |
| Random | The same random values, moving smoothly between them instead of in steps. It is the contour DRIFT follows, at a rate you set |

**Amplitude has only one square.** A tremolo only ever lowers the level set by the fader, so a unipolar shape has no second direction to go in. The one square switches across the whole depth. For the same reason, every amplitude shape starts a quarter of a cycle ahead. A note begins at full level and then dips, instead of starting half attenuated.

The square and stepped shapes do not click. A partial's gain changes smoothly across each control block instead of jumping, so each edge takes about two thirds of a millisecond. That is short enough to sound like an edge and long enough not to be heard as a click.

LINK does not change the shapes. It moves a value across the series along a weighted curve, and a list of named shapes cannot be weighted. Instead, the shape menu can set every channel at once.

**Shared by all notes** is the other entry in that menu, one for each of the two modulators. It is also the switch beside each SHAPE caption on the left of the mixer, marked with three strokes joining into one. By default each note has its own modulator. Play a chord one note at a time and you get three tremolos, each starting when its own key went down, so they move out of step. With the entry ticked, the modulator belongs to the channel instead. A note that arrives late joins the modulation already running, so the chord moves as one however it was played. An instrument with a single tremolo circuit behaves like this, which is why [Wurli](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/presets/) ships with its tremolo shared and StyloPoly with its vibrato.

Each channel keeps its own rate and shape either way. Sharing gives one modulator per channel, not one for the whole instrument, so a patch built on thirty-two rates that never line up still sounds the same with the switch on. The switch is part of the patch, so a preset saves it. Both switches are off unless a patch turns them on.

The switch lights when its modulator is shared, so a preset with a shared tremolo shows it on the panel as well as in the menu. There is one switch per modulator, and it applies to all thirty-three channels.

## Velocity and pressure, per partial

Because velocity is set per partial, a soft note can have a different timbre, not just a lower level. Set the fundamental to 0% and the upper partials to 100%, and the tone gets brighter as you play harder. A struck string or bar behaves roughly like this.

Both controls go either side of zero. A positive amount makes harder or heavier playing louder. A negative amount inverts that, so the partial is loudest when you play softly. The two halves mirror each other exactly, so -50% at a given velocity matches +50% at the opposite velocity. The negative half is useful for crossfading. Give one set of partials a positive amount and another set a negative one, and the two timbres swap places across the velocity range instead of one just fading in.

Aftertouch works the same way but **adds** to the fader instead of scaling it, and it ignores velocity. A strip with its fader all the way down is silent until you press into the key, and then it fades in. A negative amount fades an open strip out instead. Both channel pressure and polyphonic aftertouch are accepted, and the higher of the two is used. Pressure is smoothed over about 15 ms, so the steps of seven-bit MIDI are not heard in the gain.

By default the mod wheel also works as aftertouch, because most keyboards have no aftertouch and the wheel is close to hand. A wheel left at rest reads zero, so nothing changes on a controller that does send pressure. To use only one or the other, choose it in the "Aftertouch from" entry in Settings.

## The two-part envelope

Delay, attack, decay and sustain while the key is down. Releasing the key runs a small envelope of its own instead of just fading out. The KEY OFF rows set the level the sound moves to when the key is released, and how long it takes to get there. Only then does the release run from that level down to silence.

A key-off level above the sustain gives a release click or swell, like the sound of a damper landing or a hammer returning, and it can be louder than the held note. *Drawbar Organ* uses it this way: the upper drawbars jump to 55% for two milliseconds as the contacts break. A level below the sustain gives the fast drop into a long tail that a piano or a struck bell has, which is probably the more common use. A key-off level of zero skips the stage and releases from the current level.

**How fast you release the key scales that tail**, on a keyboard that can sense release velocity. The fastest release doubles the level, the slowest halves it, and 64 leaves it unchanged. It scales the level the tail starts from. On a patch with its own key-off level it changes that level, and on a patch without one it changes the sustain. It has no knob and no parameter, because like velocity it belongs to how you play, not to the patch. A fast release cannot raise a partial that is already at full level, since the envelope stops at full scale.

Most keyboards cannot sense release velocity, and on those nothing changes. They send either a note-off with a velocity of zero or a note-on with a velocity of zero in its place. Both are read as no information, not as the slowest possible release.

The delay stage keeps a partial silent before its attack begins. Setting different delays across the series makes the spectrum build up gradually instead of arriving all at once. This is how *Slow Pad* and *Shimmer* open up. The delay is fixed in samples at note-on, so moving the knob does not change the timing of a note already waiting.

**ATTACK goes below its shortest time.** Turned below 0.2 ms, it sets where in its cycle the partial starts instead of a time. This runs from 0°, a rising zero crossing, to 90° at the bottom of the knob, which starts the partial at its peak with no attack at all. A zero crossing is the softest possible start. A partial cannot reach its peak until a quarter of its period has passed, and below about 500 Hz that is longer than the shortest attack. So on most of the keyboard, where the cycle starts shapes the start of a note more than the envelope does. One millisecond into an A1, a partial starting from the zero crossing is a third of the way up, one starting from 45° is nine tenths of the way up, and one starting from the peak is all the way up. This part of the knob's ring is marked with dots instead of ticks, so you can see at a glance whether a knob is set in degrees or in milliseconds.

Like every row, it is set per channel, so some partials can start sharply and others not. LINK can spread it across the series in one drag. If every partial starts at its peak at the same time, the result is a spike: for 32 partials on a falling series, the first sample is about four times the steady peak, and the output stage has to handle it. Spreading the start points across the channels keeps the sharp start without the spike. With phase reset off in Settings, a partial carries on from wherever its cycle was, and this part of the knob acts as the shortest attack. The noise channel has no cycle to start, so its ATTACK stops at 0.2 ms.

**STRIKE** is at the top of the section because it is about how hard the key is struck, not about the shape of the envelope. It applies velocity to the two rows below it, the way the velocity row applies it to the fader. At zero it has no effect. A positive amount makes a hard note start sooner and rise faster, and makes a soft note wait and then rise slowly. A negative amount inverts this.

The two act in opposite directions on purpose, so each knob stays the limit of its own row. Velocity only ever lengthens the attack, so ATTACK is always the fastest the partial can rise. It only ever shortens the delay, so DELAY is always the latest the partial can arrive. At full amount both cover eight octaves, a range of 256 to 1. A partial set to a 2 ms attack rises in 2 ms when struck hardest and takes half a second when struck softest. A 400 ms delay stays 400 ms when struck softest and drops to under two milliseconds when struck hardest. The lengthened attack stops at five seconds, the longest the ATTACK row goes. STRIKE moves the whole row, including the part below the shortest time. A partial set to start at its peak starts there when struck hard, nearer the zero crossing when struck more lightly, and past it into a short attack when struck softest. A quarter turn is worth two octaves of attack, so at full amount the softest note turns a start at the peak into an attack of about 13 ms.

Because it is set per partial, it does more than a velocity curve for the whole instrument. Give the upper partials a strike amount and leave the fundamental at zero. A hard chord then arrives all at once and bright, while a soft one builds up, with the fundamental first and the upper partials after it.

One useful shape is the one a music box or a thumb piano has. Set no sustain at all, so the partial decays to silence while the key is still down, and then set a key-off level that brings it back. Decaying to zero does not end the note.

## Ganging the channels

**One button at the top of the caption column on the left** sets what a drag in the mixer does. Instead of a word, it shows the pointer you will get: a plain arrow, an arrow with two chain links, or an arrow with a drawn contour. Click it to see the three by name. A right-click anywhere in the mixer opens the same menu.

**Link** gangs the strips: dragging any knob moves the same knob on the other strips. It works relatively. It adds an offset to each strip's current value instead of setting them all to one value, so a spectrum you have shaped by hand keeps its shape. The offset is always measured from the values at the start of the drag, so moving the knob back to where you started restores the strips exactly, even if some of them hit the end of their range along the way.

Which channels a drag reaches, and how the movement is shared between them, are set in the same menu, under the three tools. With Link chosen, pointing at a knob lights every knob a drag from it would move, before you click. How brightly each one lights follows the curve.

**Draw** is the third tool. Dragging across the faders sets each channel you pass over to the pointer's height, so you can draw a spectrum in one stroke instead of one fader at a time. Holding shift does the same whatever tool is chosen, and the button shows the contour while the key is down. Either way, the button shows what a drag would do.

Drawing is different from Link. Link shares one relative move across the channels by a rule, and drawing sets absolute values freehand, so neither can do the other's job. Channels the pointer skips over between one moment and the next are filled in, so a fast drag leaves no gaps, and the whole stroke is a single undo step. Drawing works on the faders only, because a fader's value is its height and a pointer's height means nothing for a knob.

While drawing is armed, every fader lights in the same accent colour as the button, so you can see what the next drag would reach before you click, the same way Link previews its knobs. The pointer becomes a pencil. If you hold shift with another tool chosen, the button shows the pencil while the key is down and goes back to your tool when you let go.

| Scope | Reaches |
|---|---|
| All | every partial |
| Same interval | only the strips sharing the interval class of the one you grab, so you can move just the fifths, or just the octaves |
| Odd harmonics | 1, 3, 5 and so on, the half of the series that sounds hollow |
| Even harmonics | 2, 4, 6 and so on |

| Curve | How the drag is shared out |
|---|---|
| Uniform | every selected strip moves by the same amount |
| Taper from the grab | a strip moves less the further along the series it sits from the one you grabbed |
| Spread / gather | dragging up spreads the strips apart in random directions, dragging down pulls them together onto the strip you are dragging |

Taper is centred on the strip you grabbed, which always moves by the full amount of the drag, because the knob under the mouse has to follow the mouse. From there, each strip's share falls off in a straight line with distance, reaching nothing thirty-one channels away.

So the channel you grab sets the shape. Grab channel 1 and the movement tilts down across the full width of the mixer, from the full amount to nothing. Grab channel 32 and it tilts up instead. Grab channel 10 and the curve peaks at that channel and falls away on both sides, to 0.71 at channel 1 and 0.29 at channel 32. Distance is measured against the full width, not against the nearer end, so the reach is the same wherever you grab. Scaling it to the nearer end would make a grab on channel 2 drop channel 1 to nothing in a single step.

LINK gangs the 32 partials only. The noise channel has no tuning, pitch modulation or drift to gang.

## Working the panel

**Double-clicking a knob resets it to its default**, which is that control's own default, not the bottom of its range. On a fader that is 0 dB, not silence.

**Undo and redo** matter more here than on a smaller instrument, because one LINK drag moves the same knob on all 32 channels. Without undo, the only way back would be to reload the preset. Each step is a whole gesture, not a single value change, so that drag is undone in one step, not thirty-two. Cmd-Z and Cmd-Shift-Z, or Ctrl with the same keys on other systems, work when the host passes them on. Many hosts do not, because a DAW usually keeps those keys for its own undo. Both are also near the top of the Settings menu, and that always works. Loading a session starts with an empty undo history.

**Hovering over a strip** shows the partial it belongs to: the harmonic number, the interval that harmonic makes with the fundamental, how many semitones above the played note its tempered position is, and how far the exact ratio is from that in cents. It is that channel's row in [the table of the series](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/), shown in the mixer. The mute and solo buttons show which harmonic they would silence.

**Right-clicking anywhere in the mixer** opens the LINK menu. On the mute and solo buttons, a right-click clears every mute or every solo at once instead.

## Reading the mixer

### The two readouts

Each channel shows two figures: the cents set by its tuning knob and the level of its fader. Both are drawn as seven-segment displays instead of text, so a number the instrument reports looks different from a number you typed. Two of the readings are not numbers. A partial left in equal temperament reads **Et**, and a fader all the way down reads **-inF**. The fundamental and the octaves read **0.0**, because their just interval is the note itself. As on a real display, each has a fixed row of cells whose segments are either lit or unlit, so the figures are always the same size.

### Lamps on the rules

Each of the rules that divide a strip into groups has a lamp. It shows what the group below it is doing to this partial at that moment.

| Rule | Shows |
|---|---|
| PITCH MOD | a needle on a track, flat to the left and sharp to the right, showing where modulation, drift and any glide still in progress have put the partial |
| ENVELOPE | how far up its envelope the partial is, while the key is down |
| KEY OFF | the same, once the key is up and the key-off stage has taken over |
| AMP MOD | how far the tremolo has lowered the level, so it pulses at the tremolo's rate and swings further at greater depth |
| OUTPUT | two lamps side by side, one for each row below it: the left shows how much of the partial velocity has left, the right shows what pressure on the key is adding |

The lamps read the voice pool, not the knobs, so they show what a note is doing, not a setting, and nothing pulses when nothing is sounding. They follow the loudest voice on that partial, the same one the meter follows. The output rule has two lamps, one for each row below it, and each has the shape of the knob above it. VELOCITY can only reduce the level, so its lamp shows what the row leaves: full when velocity has taken nothing from the partial, dark when it has taken all of it, and full at every velocity when the knob is at the centre. AFTERTOUCH adds level instead, so its lamp is dark at rest and lights up as you press into the key, whichever direction that row is set to push. The needle's scale is fixed and the same on every strip, so you can compare two channels by eye. Full deflection is 225 cents. That covers a vibrato and a drift at full depth, but not the widest the depth knob reaches. A square set to jump an octave pushes the needle to the end of its track, and so does a wide glide until it is within a couple of semitones of its note. With a scale wide enough for an octave, an ordinary vibrato would not move the needle at all.

### Meters

Each channel meters the actual output of its partial, on a decibel scale down to -48 dB. The envelope, tremolo, velocity, aftertouch and mute or solo all show in it, and you can watch the spectrum change as a note decays. The meter fills the fader's own track instead of sitting beside it, and the fader cap is drawn as translucent glass so the meter shows through it. It shows the loudest instance of the partial across the sounding voices, not the sum, so it shows the shape of the patch instead of hitting the top as soon as you play a chord.

### Colour and hover

Channels are coloured by interval class, in chromatic order along a narrow range from blue at the octave, through magenta and red, to yellow at the major seventh, so you can pick out octaves, fifths and thirds while you scroll. The range is narrow on purpose, so 32 channels look like one family instead of a rainbow, and none of the colours overlap the green and cyan of the global controls. Pointing at a knob highlights its row across the whole mixer and marks its channel, so the control where the two meet is the one a drag would move.

### Silenced channels

A channel you cannot hear, because it is muted or because another channel is soloed, turns its lights off. Its knob rings, both readouts and the macro columns beside its fader go dark, and its waveform drawings turn grey. The pointer on each knob and the fader cap still show where they are set, and M and S stay lit, since one of them is usually what silenced it.

### Folding the mixer down

Clicking a section heading in the caption gutter folds that group of rows away on every channel at once. Clicking that section's rule on any strip does the same, so you do not have to move to the gutter and then find the partial you were working on again. Pointing at a rule shows the same hand pointer as a heading and lights that section's caption and its disclosure mark, so you can see what the click would fold before you click. The window shrinks by exactly the height of those rows. Pitch modulation, envelope, key off, amp mod and output can each be folded. The tuning at the top and the faders at the bottom always stay. A folded heading keeps its activity lamp, so a hidden group still shows whether it is doing anything. The fold state is saved with the session, not with the patch.

## The noise channel

A noise channel marked NZ sits on the right, after the series. It has the same envelope, tremolo, velocity, aftertouch, pan, mute, solo, level and meter as a partial, and takes part in solo alongside them. It is not part of the harmonic series, so it has no tuning, pitch modulation or drift of its own. COLOUR takes the place of the tuning row, and a string takes the rest.

COLOUR tilts the noise from a dark rumble at one end, through flat in the middle, to a bright hiss at the other. The middle is fully flat, not just less filtered. Each voice runs its own noise stream, so playing a chord does not layer eight copies of the identical signal.

**A string** sits under COLOUR, where a partial's pitch modulation would be, for the noise to strike. It is a Karplus-Strong string: a delay line one period of the note long, fed back through a gentle low-pass filter, so a burst of noise sent into it comes out as a plucked note that loses its high frequencies first. It is tuned to the note and follows the pitch wheel, glide and Adaptive like the fundamental does. The noise strikes it after COLOUR and the envelope have shaped the noise, so a darker colour strikes it more softly. STRING crossfades from the noise alone to the string alone. DECAY sets how long the string rings while the key is down, DAMP how quickly it loses its high frequencies, and POINT where along the string the noise strikes. POINT runs from near the end, which keeps every harmonic, to the middle, which removes the even ones.

The envelope sets how the string is played. A noise envelope a few milliseconds long plucks the string and lets it ring, like the start of a harpsichord note, or of a guitar note under the organ. A noise held on a short, dark string blows into it, which gives a pitched breath. When the key is released, the channel's RELEASE damps the string. At the top of the keyboard, where the string is too short to tune, it fades back to plain noise instead of playing out of tune. COLOUR and the string's four knobs belong only to the noise channel, so pointing at them does not light a row across the mixer. The [Space Cowboy](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/presets/#what-ships) preset plucks it for its tremolo guitar.

---

Page: Overtonium effects: character, echo, reverb, converter and CLIP
URL: https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/effects/
Last changed: 2026-10-16

# Effects

Everything on the bar along the top of the window affects the whole instrument, not a single channel: the oscillator character every partial is built from, the wobble under the series, the resonator, the drive on the bus where the channels are summed, the echo, the reverb, the converter, and the output stage with its meter.

## The signal chain

[Diagram: The order the signal passes through. Each of the thirty-three channels runs a sine partial through its envelope and key-off stage, its tremolo, its velocity and pressure amounts, its fader and its pan. The thirty-three are summed and run through the converter, the resonator and the bus drive. The mix then passes through the wobble, the echo, the reverb, the master fader and the safety clipper before it leaves. each of the thirty-three channels sine partial n envelope and key off tremolo velocity and pressure fader pan then the mix of all of them converter rate, bits resonator 88 strings bus drive wobble echo reverb master fader clipper summed out.]

The order things happen in. Everything on a channel strip runs before the channels are mixed, and everything on the bar runs after. This is why a channel meter and the output meter disagree while a tail is ringing.

[Image: The top bar: four icon buttons in two rows, settings and macros above the buttons that open the Playing and Tuning bars, then the wordmark over the loaded preset on a fourteen-segment display, the oscillator character, the stretch, track and wobble controls, the resonator with its mode and three knobs, the echo, the reverb, and the output meter with the master fader across it, two seven-segment converter readouts reading kilohertz and bits, and the output stage reading Soft.]

## Character

Chooses the oscillator that every partial uses, and is the first control in the group that sets up the series. All six are sine oscillators. They differ in how each circuit fails to make a perfect sine. **Pure** is an ideal sine that no real circuit produces. **Bulb** is a Wien bridge oscillator kept steady by a lamp. It adds no harmonics at all, but its level lags half a second behind every change of pitch, so it reacts to gestures. A vibrato is heard in the level as well as in the pitch, and a bend dips and then recovers as the lamp catches up. A held note with nothing moving sounds exactly like Pure, because the circuit's job is to hold the level steady. **Rail** is a phase-shift oscillator driven into its own supply rail. This hardens the tone with a third harmonic and no even harmonics. **Diode** is a triangle shaped into a sine by two mismatched diodes. This puts a kink in one half of the wave and adds a second, third and fourth harmonic. **Valve** is a triode biased so that one half of the wave bends over before the other. It is the only one here whose loudest added harmonic is an octave above the partial rather than a twelfth, and that is what people mean by valve warmth.

**Op-amp** is an amplifier that cannot keep up with a fast note. It is the one that changes as you play. Below a kilohertz nothing is limited and the partials are untouched. Above it they lose first their corners and then everything but their slopes, which leaves a triangle. So the top of the series gets harder as it climbs while the bottom stays the same, and a chord played high sounds like a different instrument from the same chord played low.

Because this is an additive instrument, these harmonics land among the partials you are already mixing, at exact multiples of the partial that made them. The rack's own spread, described below, moves the real partials off those exact ratios, and TUNE and STRETCH move them further. So the two beat against each other instead of adding up, and that is what makes a character sound like a circuit and not like a tone control. The harmonics are removed as a partial climbs, so nothing folds back down. A partial near the top of the range plays a plain sine whatever character is chosen.

Each character is also a rack of thirty-two oscillators, not one oscillator used thirty-two times. Units built to the same spec do not come out identical, so every character except Pure puts each partial a couple of cents and a fraction of a decibel off its target. The amount is fixed for each character, so you get the same rack every time you load the patch, in every host and on every machine. This is not DRIFT, which wanders. Partial 1 is the reference the other thirty-one were tuned against, and it stays exactly in place. So a note still lands on the key you played, and choosing a character does not change how loud the patch is. This spread is what makes the beating above happen in a patch nobody has detuned. The units also differ in how much they distort: each unit's circuit is built to one of three drives, fifteen percent either side of the nominal.

The button lights in the character's own colour, taken from the same colour band as the channel strips: yellow for Bulb, running down through the warm colours to the red of channel 3 for Op-amp. Pure does not light, because it adds nothing.

Character is part of the patch, not part of the setup, so a preset can change it and saving a preset stores it. Twenty-eight of the thirty-five [factory presets](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/presets/) use one, so most of what you load already uses a circuit, not the plain sine.

## Wobble

Makes the whole instrument sound like a warped record. The pitch is bent by reading the output back through a delay line whose length keeps changing, as happens when a platter runs off-centre or a capstan slips. There is a slow warp at about once per turn of a 33 rpm disc, a faster wander on top, and now and then a sharp slip that bends hard and settles back. The slips grow in both rate and size with the square of the control, so a low setting sounds like a tired turntable and a high one like a badly failing tape transport. It comes before the echo, so the repeats carry its wobble instead of wobbling on their own.

## Resonator

The resonator is eighty-eight sympathetic strings, one for each key of a piano from A0 to C8, that resonate with what you play. Each is a Karplus-Strong string, the same kind the noise channel strikes. They are fed the sum of the thirty-three channels, and what they ring back is mixed in before the bus drive. So the drive and everything after it treat them as part of the instrument, not as a room around it. It has its own frame on the top bar, after the character's. The RESONATOR button shows the mode and opens a menu of the five, and it is lit whenever the mode is not Off.

**Piano** works like a piano: the strings of the keys you hold are free, the rest are damped, and the sustain pedal lifts every damper. A held key's string is tuned to the pitch the key is sounding. The other strings wait at the pitch a key struck now would sound, which under Adaptive is the tuning their pitch class had last. None of them bends, because a piano's strings do not follow the wheel. **Open** is Piano with the sustain pedal always down: every string rings, and held keys ring the loudest. **Octave** is twelve strings from C3, always free, so every note finds something to ring with. **Series** is the tuning root's first eight harmonics from its second octave, tuned pure and always free. It works as a drone that responds to any note that falls on the root's own harmonic series. The root is set on the [Tuning](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/#root) bar or in Settings, and it stays available for Series under equal temperament too.

**MIX** goes from the instrument alone to the resonator alone, as on the echo and the reverb. On a held chord the level stays about the same as you turn it up. At 100 % only the resonator is left, so short notes lose their attack there. **DECAY** sets how long a free string rings, from 200 ms to 10 s. The level stays about the same at any setting. **DAMP** sets how quickly the high end dies away. A damper stops its string over 0.8 s at the bottom of the keyboard and 0.25 s at the top, or sooner if DECAY is shorter, so a released bass key leaves the short hum of a felt damper on a heavy string. A string freed only by the pedal gets much less of the signal than a held key's string, so the pedal adds a bloom under a chord instead of making it louder.

The resonator is part of the patch. Metallic Piano and Space Cowboy use it, and the other factory presets have it off. With eight voices it uses about one percent of a core with the pedal up, and about five percent with every string freed by the pedal.

## Bus drive

The thirty-three channels are not just added together. They are summed onto a bus with drive, by an amount and in a style set by the oscillator character. So a patch gets louder into the same kind of saturation a mixing desk would give it. It responds to level, not to a setting: play quietly and it is barely there, play hard and you hear it. Pure sums cleanly and adds nothing. There is no knob, because the amount is part of the character you choose.

## Echo

Three machines behind one button, and the button shows which one is running. **Tape** is a loop with two motors. Moving the time knob makes the tape speed up or slow down to the new setting instead of jumping to it, so the repeats slide in pitch on the way. The two paths run at slightly different speeds, so a repeat comes back doubled rather than bounced. **BBD** is a bucket brigade delay. It loses its high end because a bucket brigade is a sampler with almost no filtering, and it sweeps as the clock wanders. **Digital** is a clean delay: what goes in comes back out, later and quieter, crossing to the other side on every repeat. It is the only ping-pong of the three.

When the echo is off, its knobs keep their settings, but their rings go dark and only the pointer on each knob shows where it is set. The reverb and the resonator do the same when they are off.

AGE means something different on each machine. On the tape it is wear: the high end lost on every pass, how far the motor wanders, and how hard the tape saturates. On the BBD it is the clock slowing down and how much the companding breathes. On the digital it is bits and sample rate, so a tail starts as the clean signal and ends as a degraded copy of it. The tape never reaches zero wear, because a transport that held speed exactly would put the repeat back in mono, and no real transport holds speed exactly.

## Reverb

Three machines again, on the same kind of button. **Room** is a feedback delay network whose room size follows its decay time, because a long tail in a small room sounds like a spring, not a space. **Modulated plate** is a sheet of steel with no shape you can hear, so a hit spreads across all of it at once and the tail is dense from the start instead of building up in stages. Its allpass filters move further than a real plate's would, which is why the menu calls it modulated. Without that movement, a long decay repeats its own pattern instead of washing out. **Spring** is a tray of coiled springs. A coil carries high frequencies faster than low ones, so a hit comes back as a chirp that starts high and falls. Every bounce adds another chirp, so a spring sounds less like what you played as it decays, not just quieter.

DECAY, DAMP and PRE mean the same on all three and are matched, so switching machines changes the character of a tail but not its length or loudness. On the plate, DAMP is the sheet losing its high end to the air. On the spring, it is the spring's own loss each time the signal crosses the tray.

## The converter

Shown as two seven-segment readouts under the output meter. Turning the sample rate down really lowers the rate, it is not a filter on top. The whole voice pool renders at the lower rate, which costs a fifth as much at 8 kHz, and partials above the new ceiling fold back down instead of disappearing.

## CLIP

Five machines behind one button, on the finished output after the master fader, so the master fader sets how hard they are driven. The fader and the choice are both saved with the preset, so how hard a patch drives this stage is part of the patch. **Soft** is linear up to seven tenths and then rounds off, gradually and symmetrically. Every preset is balanced for Soft. **Hard** is a wall at full scale: nothing happens until the signal reaches it. It sounds like a converter with no headroom left. **Asymmetric** lets one half of the wave bend over before the other, as a single-ended stage does. Soft and Hard treat both halves the same and add odd harmonics. Asymmetric adds even ones, so it sounds different, not just louder. **Limiter** does not change the shape of the wave. It turns the level down as the signal approaches the ceiling and lets it back up afterwards. **Fold** folds the wave back on itself instead of flattening it. This makes far more harmonics than the others, and they move with the level, so it sounds tonal where the others crunch.

Off lets the output go past full scale and reach the host unchanged. Use it when something later in the chain catches the peaks. None of the five lets the output past full scale. That limit is the purpose of the stage, not a side effect of the shapes, and each shape stays within it however hard it is driven. The button shortens Asymmetric to ASYM and Limiter to LIMIT to fit, while the menu and your host's automation lane show the full names. It sits under the meter with the converter readouts, because together they are everything that happens to the signal on its way out. The switch is also in the Settings menu.

With **Limiter lookahead** switched on in the Settings menu, the Limiter looks two milliseconds ahead. The gain reduction is already in place when the peak arrives, instead of following it, and that is what makes it a true limiter and not a clipper. This adds latency. A plugin whose latency changed with the preset would make the host rebuild its processing graph every time, so the latency applies to all five shapes and to the stage when it is off. Overtonium reports 108 samples at 48 kHz, a little over two milliseconds, which your host compensates for on playback.

**It is off by default**, and the plugin then reports only the bus stage's 12 samples. Only the Limiter uses the lookahead and no factory preset uses the Limiter, so with it on everyone else would pay two milliseconds for nothing. The limiter still works with it off. The detector sees a single sample instead of a window, so the gain is exact and immediate and the ceiling still holds. But the smoothing is lost, and a gain that jumps in steps is a distortion in itself, about fifteen times as much. It is in Settings and not on the bar because nothing a preset can change is allowed to change what the plugin reports to your host. If you rely on the Limiter and want it smooth, switch it on. Most hosts pick up the new figure while running, and some only when playback stops or on reload, so choose before a take, not during one.

## The output meter

Horizontal, and split into left and right. The two channels are identical until something is panned off centre, and a single summed meter would hide exactly that. It reads the finished output after master gain and the clipper. The lamps run from teal through amber to orange as they approach full scale. Each colour is fixed to its decibel position instead of stretching with the level. A scale below is marked at -48, -36, -24, -12, -6 and 0 dB. Each bar holds its peak for a couple of seconds.

---

Page: Playing Overtonium: MPE, automation, macros and MIDI Learn
URL: https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/
Last changed: 2026-10-15

# Playing

How to play the instrument and control it from outside the window: MPE, legato and glide, the Playing and Tuning bars, the Settings menu, automation from a host with every parameter listed, macros that move a whole row from one control, and MIDI Learn for playing it from a controller.

## MPE

Off by default. It is in Settings and in the Playing bar. With MPE on, a controller that gives every note its own MIDI channel can bend and press each note separately. On this instrument, that means each finger gets its own copy of all 33 aftertouch destinations. Press into one note in a chord and only that note's upper partials come in.

Slide, the forward and back movement of a finger on the key, has its own destination setting in Settings and in the Playing bar. By default it changes that note's brightness, thinning or opening up the top of the series, which is what players expect from that axis. It can control the tuning instead, so that pushing one finger forward moves that note alone [between equal temperament and just intonation](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/) while the rest of the chord stays where it is. A keyboard without a slide axis sends nothing, so nothing changes.

Slide is read as movement, not as a position. The first value a note receives becomes that note's zero, and what affects the sound is how far the axis has moved from it since. This is because controllers handle the axis differently. A Seaboard reports where the finger is and rests at the centre. An Expressive E Osmose uses the first part of the key travel for pressure and only then starts sending slide, from the bottom of its range upward. Read as a position, the Osmose would jump the moment the axis starts sending. Read as movement, both start the note as the patch sets it and follow the finger from there.

The movement is scaled so that the longer of the two directions from the resting point covers the full slide, and both directions use that same rate. A resting point near the bottom of the axis leaves very little room below it. Giving that small range its own scale would make it far too sensitive: pressing in would feel smooth, but coming back out would jump straight to dark. So the short side has the same sensitivity as the long side and reaches less far.

MPE is a setting, not always on, because it changes what a channel number means. With it off, the channel is ignored: a key-up on channel 7 releases a note that started on channel 1, which is what a single-channel keyboard needs. With it on, the channel is part of the note's identity, so the same key can be held on two channels at once and bent in two directions, as two voices instead of one retriggering the other.

## Legato

A switch in Settings and in the Playing bar, beside the voice count. What it does depends on that count. **With one voice** the instrument is monophonic. Pressing a key while another is still held moves the note instead of starting it again, so the envelopes continue and a run keeps the shape the first key gave it, without restarting the attack. Releasing a key while others are still held goes back to the most recent of them, which makes trills work. Only releasing the last key releases the note.

**With more than one voice it plays a top line.** A key pressed above every held note except the highest one continues that highest note's phrase. It starts its own voice, which takes over the highest note's envelopes at their current point and glides from its pitch, so the sound does not start again. Every other key plays as normal. This means you can play a legato melody over a staccato chord. The chord retriggers each time its keys are released and pressed again, and the melody carries on from note to note above it, up or down, as long as it stays above the chord.

A legato melody over chords played below it, two notes to a bar, one with the chord and one in between. It is played softly on Synth Ensemble, where each new note takes about half a second to swell in. With Legato off, every note of the melody swells in again. With it on and eight voices, the melody carries on from note to note, with or without the chord, while the chords still swell in underneath.

**Legato off**

**Legato on**

The note a melody carries on from is never cut off, so a key that turns out to be part of the chord always sounds. It keeps sounding while its key is down and fades quickly when the key is released, instead of playing its full release under the melody. The same goes for the upper note of a trill when you return to the lower key.

A key pressed below the highest note could be the melody stepping down, or a chord played under a held melody. Only what the previous melody key does next would tell them apart, so the instrument goes by what is most likely. Above the highest note, a key always carries on. Below it, with a chord held and no other key just struck, it carries on if it is above that chord, however far down it goes. Alone under a single melody note, or among keys struck together, it carries on only if it is within a major third and is the highest of the keys struck with it. A melody usually moves by seconds and thirds, and the top of a chord usually sits further down. A wrong guess costs no more than a new attack. No key is ever delayed.

When the instrument runs out of voices, the melody is the last voice taken. The sustain pedal holds the sound but not the melody, so a note held only by the pedal does not carry anything on. With MPE on it works the same way, and a note carried onto a key on its own channel takes on that key's bend, pressure and slide.

Legato moves the note in a single step. With a [glide](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#glide) time on the channels, it slides there instead.

## Glide

**Every channel has its own glide**, the last knob under PITCH MOD. It sets how long that partial takes to move from the previous note to the new one, from Off, the default on every channel, to five seconds. Because each partial has its own time, the partials do not have to arrive together. Short times on the upper partials and a long one on the fundamental bring the brightness in first, with the pitch following. The other way round, the pitch arrives first and the tone follows. With settings in between, the partials stop agreeing on a fundamental while they move and settle on one as they arrive. A single portamento cannot do this.

The same phrase twice on the [Glide](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/presets/) preset: up a fifth, up a fourth and down the octave. With every glide at zero, each note arrives straight away. With the preset's settings, from nothing on the fundamental to two and a half seconds on the thirty-second partial, the pitch arrives at once and you can hear the upper partials still moving.

**Glide off**

**Glide on**

A partial glides in a straight line in pitch, and everything that depends on pitch follows the glide. The oscillator character is chosen for the frequency the partial has reached, and the Bulb character's lamp lags behind a long slide as a real lamp would. Vibrato, drift and both kinds of bend are added on top. The needle on each partial's PITCH MOD rule follows the glide and swings back to centre as the partial arrives, so with different glide times you can watch the partials arrive one at a time.

**Two switches control every channel at once.** They are the two letters **L** and **T** beside the GLIDE caption on the left of the mixer. They are also at the end of the menu that opens when you right-click any GLIDE knob, under *Glide (every channel)*. A letter is lit when its switch is on. The switches are part of the patch, so a preset saves them and a legato lead can set them. The letters show their state as soon as a preset loads.

| Switch | Choices | What it decides |
|---|---|---|
| When, L | Always, the default, or Legato (L lit) | Always glides from the last note played, even if its key was released long ago. Legato glides only when the new key is pressed while another key is still held, so a phrase played detached jumps to each note and the same phrase played legato slides between them. A note held only by the sustain pedal does not count as held |
| What the time means, T | Fixed rate, the default, or Fixed time (T lit) | Fixed rate makes the time the length of a slide over one octave, so a fifth takes a little over half of it and two octaves take twice as long, like a finger sliding along a string at a steady speed. Fixed time makes every slide take the set time however far it goes, so a leap and a step arrive at the same moment |

Played polyphonically, each new note glides from the last note played. In [Legato](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#legato), the voice carrying the phrase glides from wherever it is: the single voice when one voice is set, and the top line when more are set. A key pressed halfway through a slide reverses it from the current point instead of jumping to either end. A trill that returns to a key still held also glides back to it.

GLIDE is a row like any other, so [LINK](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/controls/#link) sets it across the series in one drag and a [macro](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#macros) can change every channel's glide time from one control.

## The Playing and Tuning bars

The lower two of the four buttons at the left end of the top bar, a keyboard and a tuning fork, each open a bar between the top bar and the mixer. The bars hold the settings you change while playing, as opposed to the ones you set once. Both bars start closed, and each instance remembers which are open. A bar takes its height from the mixer, which scrolls, so the window stays the same size. If the window is already at its minimum height, it grows by the height of the bar.

**Playing** has the voice count with IN USE, which shows how many voices are sounding, release tails included. Beside them are Legato and No stack, the pitch bend range, and MPE with Aftertouch from and Slide to. After these it shows what your hands are doing. SUSTAIN lights while the pedal is down. PITCH shows the pitch wheel's position from the centre against the bend range, or with MPE on, the key bent furthest. WHEEL and PRESSURE fill from the left. PRESSURE shows the keyboard's own pressure, from the channel or from the key pressed hardest, so the wheel moves only WHEEL even when Aftertouch from follows it. Last are the eight [macros](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#macros) as knobs in their colours. Each is named after the row it controls and turns by the same amount as its slider in MACROS. A macro not yet made shows a blank knob with its number. Right-click a knob to assign its macro, to edit it in MACROS, or to bind a controller to it. **Tuning** has the temperament, root and reference pitch, and under Adaptive, the drift beside them. Under Adaptive it also has a NO DRIFT switch that keeps the keyboard home, a 7:4 switch for the harmonic seventh, a PURE lamp and the Retune knob. Together they show [what Adaptive is doing](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/#adaptive) to the chord you hold. Last are twelve displays, one for each note, showing how far it is from equal temperament in cents, with the white keys on a lighter background as on a keyboard. Each setting's display opens the same list as its entry in Settings, and each switch lights while it is on, so a bar is another way to reach the same settings, not a separate copy of them. If the window is too narrow for a whole bar, the bar wraps onto more rows like the top bar does, and takes the extra height from the mixer.

[Image: The Playing bar with C7 held on the pedal: eight voices with four in use, Legato off and No stack lit, a bend range of 2 semitones, MPE off with aftertouch from Either and slide to Brightness, SUSTAIN lit, the pitch wheel at rest in the middle, the mod wheel and pressure part way up, and three macros made, Level in red, Pitch mod depth in green and Release in blue, followed by five blank knobs numbered 4 to 8.] [Image: The Tuning bar under Adaptive with C7 held: the temperament reading Adaptive on a root of C at 440 Hz with a drift of 0, NO DRIFT off, 7:4 lit, PURE lit and the Retune knob near its start, then twelve displays for the notes, C, E, G and B flat lit at 15.4, 1.7, 17.1 and minus 15.8 cents, the white keys on a light ground.]

## The Settings menu

Settings you set once and then leave. The menu is where you set up the instrument, and the panel is where you make the sound, so where a control sits tells you which kind it is. The ones you change while playing are also in [the Playing and Tuning bars](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#bars).

| Entry | Choices | What it decides |
|---|---|---|
| Overtonium X is available... |  | Only there when a newer version is out, above the version. It opens the release on GitHub, and SETTINGS stays lit until you update |
| Which version this is |  | A heading near the top of the menu, not an entry, because it describes the build and is not a choice. A bug report asks for this number |
| Check for new versions | off by default | The only entry that connects to anything outside your computer. [What it sends](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/install/) is only a request for a file |
| Undo, Redo |  | The same steps as Cmd-Z, for hosts that keep that shortcut for themselves |
| Polyphony | 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 or 16 voices. 8 by default | How many notes can sound at once |
| No stack | on by default | Playing a key again takes over the note it is already sounding instead of adding a second copy, as a string or a bar does. When off, every strike gets its own voice and the tails add up, so a bell struck repeatedly builds up |
| Legato | off by default | With one voice, a key pressed while another is held moves the note without starting it again. With more voices, the highest held note does this for a key above the rest, and everything below it plays as normal. See [Legato](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/playing/#legato) |
| Pitch bend range | 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 12 or 24 semitones. 2 by default | How far the wheel bends. Only the commonly used ranges are offered, not all twenty-five |
| MPE | off by default | Whether a note's channel is part of its identity, which lets pitch bend and pressure work per note |
| Aftertouch from | Channel pressure, Mod wheel, Either. Either by default | What drives the AT row on every strip. Polyphonic aftertouch is not on the list because it is always routed, whatever this is set to |
| Slide to | Off, Brightness, Tuning. Brightness by default | What the forward and back movement of an MPE finger controls |
| Temperament, Root, Reference pitch | Seven temperaments, twelve roots, 415 to 466 Hz | What the keyboard is tuned to, as explained in [the tuning system](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/). Root is greyed out for equal temperament, which has no centre |
| Retune | Fast, 30 ms, the default, or Smooth, 300 ms | How long a held note takes to slide to its new tuning when the [Adaptive](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/#adaptive) temperament retunes the chord around it. These are two quick settings for the Retune knob in the Tuning bar, which runs from an instant jump at zero up to one second. Greyed out for every other temperament |
| Harmonic sevenths | on by default | Whether Adaptive tunes a minor seventh 7:4 above its root, the harmonic seventh, when nothing else in the chord would beat against it. When off, every seventh has the size the chain of fifths gives it. Also the 7:4 switch in the Tuning bar. Greyed out for every other temperament |
| No drift | off by default | Whether Adaptive keeps the chord you hold as close to home as it can. When on, a progression that would shift the keyboard by a comma moves a held note by a comma instead, and a key played after silence goes home. When off, the keyboard follows the music, up to two commas either way. Also the NO DRIFT switch in the Tuning bar. Greyed out for every other temperament |
| Phase reset | on by default | When a note begins from silence, starts each partial at the point its ATTACK sets: a rising zero crossing, or nearer its peak when the attack is turned below its shortest time. When off, a partial carries on from wherever its cycle was |
| Safety clip | on by default | Whether the output stage at the end of the chain is on. Best left on when you push 32 faders up. Which of its five shapes it uses is chosen on the bar, under the meter |
| Limiter lookahead | off by default | Whether the Limiter can look ahead at the incoming signal. On makes it smoother but adds two milliseconds of latency on every shape. Only the Limiter uses the lookahead, but the latency must not change with the patch. The only setting here that changes what the plugin reports to your host |
| Zoom | 75, 100, 125 or 150% | How big the window is on your screen. It sits at the bottom with the entry below it, because everything above these two is about the instrument and these are not |
| Fit all 32 channels |  | Resets the window to the width that shows the whole mixer, and to the height your unfolded rows need. A window remembers the size you dragged it to, so a narrow window opens narrow in every later session. This entry resets it |

Almost none of these settings are saved in a [preset](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/presets/). This is a rule, not a list that might get out of date: how you play the instrument and what it is tuned to belong to the session, not to any one sound in it. For the same reason, presets do not save the zoom, the window size or which groups of rows you have folded away.

The safety clip is the exception in this table, and the master fader is the exception outside it. The output stage has five shapes to choose from, and the master fader sets how hard the signal drives into it, so how hard a patch drives that stage is part of the patch, not of your setup. As a result, **loading a preset changes your output level**.

## Automating it from the host

Eight hundred and fifty parameters reach the host: forty-four global ones, twenty-three on each of the 32 partials, twenty-two on the noise channel, and six for each of the eight macros. They are listed in the same order as the panel, with the globals first, then each channel in turn, and the noise channel last.

Every per-channel name includes its channel, so you can search a parameter list either way. Type `H7` to find that partial, or type `Tune` to find that row across the whole mixer. A screen reader reads the same names, which is why they are words, not numbers.

| What you are after | What the host calls it |
|---|---|
| The master fader | `Master` |
| The seventh partial's tuning | `H7 Tune` |
| The eleventh partial's fader | `H11 Level` |
| The noise channel's brightness | `Noise Colour` |
| How long the echo's repeats are | `Echo Time` |

The noise channel has twenty-two instead of twenty-three because it has no tuning, pitch modulation, drift or glide, and has COLOUR and the four knobs of its string instead.

Everything in Settings is in the list too, even though no preset changes it. The temperament, the polyphony and the bend range can all be automated, so a host can change the temperament partway through a piece.

**Each parameter is identified by its own id, not by its position**, in the Audio Unit and in the VST3. This lets a release add controls without breaking automation you have already written. 1.6.0 added 65 new parameters among the existing ones, not after them, and every automation lane written before it still points at the same control.

LINK is not a parameter, because it is a mouse tool, not part of the sound. A LINK drag starts a gesture on every channel it reaches, writes each one, and ends them all together, so the host records what actually moved: thirty-two lanes if the drag moved thirty-two channels.

### Every parameter

All 850 as the host lists them, with a control that every partial or every macro carries given one row for all of them. The range and the default are what the plugin itself shows. The same list, one parameter per line with its id, is [parameters.json](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/parameters.json), written by the plugin rather than by hand.

**Global**, forty-four of them.

| What the host calls it | Id | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Master` | `masterGain` | -60.0 to 12.0 dB | -12.0 dB |
| `Polyphony` | `polyphony` | Legato, 1 voice, 2 voices, 4 voices, 6 voices, 8 voices, 12 voices, 16 voices | 8 voices |
| `No Stack` | `oneVoicePerKey` | Off or on | On |
| `Pitch Bend Range` | `bendRange` | 0 to 24 | 2 |
| `Phase Reset` | `phaseReset` | Off or on | On |
| `Safety Clip` | `safetyClip` | Off or on | On |
| `Lookahead` | `lookahead` | Off or on | Off |
| `MPE` | `mpe` | Off or on | Off |
| `Stretch` | `stretch` | -1200 ct to +1200 ct | Harmonic |
| `Tracking` | `track` | Off to 12.0 dB/oct | Off |
| `Character` | `character` | Pure, Bulb, Rail, Diode, Valve, Op-amp | Pure |
| `Wobble` | `wobble` | 0 % to 100 % | 0 % |
| `Temperament` | `temperament` | Equal, Just (major), Pythagorean, Quarter-comma meantone, Werckmeister III, Young, Adaptive | Equal |
| `Tuning Root` | `tuningRoot` | C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, A#, B | C |
| `Reference Pitch` | `referenceHz` | A = 415 Hz, A = 430 Hz, A = 432 Hz, A = 435 Hz, A = 438 Hz, A = 440 Hz, A = 442 Hz, A = 443 Hz, A = 444 Hz, A = 446 Hz, A = 466 Hz | A = 440 Hz |
| `Aftertouch From` | `atSource` | Channel pressure, Mod wheel, Either | Either |
| `Slide To` | `slideDest` | Off, Brightness, Tuning | Brightness |
| `Sample Rate` | `lofiRate` | Host, 32 kHz, 22.050 kHz, 16 kHz, 11.025 kHz, 8 kHz, 6 kHz, 4 kHz | Host |
| `Bit Depth` | `lofiBits` | Host, 16 bit, 12 bit, 10 bit, 8 bit, 6 bit, 4 bit, 3 bit, 2 bit | Host |
| `Echo` | `echoOn` | Off or on | Off |
| `Echo Mix` | `echoMix` | 0 % to 100 % | 25 % |
| `Echo Time` | `echoTime` | 20.0 ms to 2.00 s | 350 ms |
| `Echo Feedback` | `echoFeedback` | 0 % to 95 % | 35 % |
| `Echo Age` | `echoAge` | 0 % to 100 % | 29 % |
| `Reverb` | `reverbOn` | Off or on | Off |
| `Reverb Mix` | `reverbMix` | 0 % to 100 % | 25 % |
| `Reverb Decay` | `reverbDecay` | 200 ms to 20.00 s | 2.00 s |
| `Reverb Damping` | `reverbDamp` | 0 % to 100 % | 50 % |
| `Reverb Pre-delay` | `reverbPreDelay` | 0.0 ms to 250 ms | 0.0 ms |
| `Pitch Mod Shared` | `pmInPhase` | Off or on | Off |
| `Amp Mod Shared` | `amInPhase` | Off or on | Off |
| `Echo Type` | `echoType` | Tape, Bucket brigade, Digital | Tape |
| `Clip Type` | `clipType` | Soft, Hard, Asymmetric, Limiter, Fold | Soft |
| `Reverb Type` | `reverbType` | Room, Modulated Plate, Spring | Room |
| `Glide Trigger` | `glideTrigger` | Always, Legato | Always |
| `Glide Mode` | `glideMode` | Fixed rate, Fixed time | Fixed rate |
| `Legato` | `legato` | Off or on | Off |
| `Adaptive Retune` | `adaptiveRetune` | 0.0 ms to 1.00 s | 30.0 ms |
| `Adaptive Harmonic Sevenths` | `adaptiveSeventh` | Off or on | On |
| `Adaptive No Drift` | `adaptiveHome` | Off or on | Off |
| `Resonator Mode` | `resonatorMode` | Off, Piano, Open, Octave, Series | Off |
| `Resonator Mix` | `resonatorMix` | 0 % to 100 % | 50 % |
| `Resonator Decay` | `resonatorDecay` | 200 ms to 10.00 s | 4.00 s |
| `Resonator Damp` | `resonatorDamp` | 0 % to 100 % | 40 % |

**On every partial**, twenty-three controls, each one on all 32 partials.

| `Macro 1 Curve to Macro 8 Curve` | `macro1_curve to macro8_curve` | Uniform, Taper | Uniform |
| `Macro 1 Anchor to Macro 8 Anchor` | `macro1_anchor to macro8_anchor` | 1 to 32 | 1 |
| `Macro 1 Colour to Macro 8 Colour` | `macro1_colour to macro8_colour` | None, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Cyan, Blue, Violet, Magenta | Differs by macro, Red on Macro 1 to Magenta on Macro 8 |

## Macros

**A macro is one parameter that moves a whole row.** Macros exist for automation. A Link drag across the tuning knobs moves 32 parameters, and a host records only the last one you touched, so a change across the row that you can make by hand cannot be recorded. A macro gives that change a single control that a host can automate.

The icon of three faders on the top bar, beside the settings cog, opens the macros over the mixer. Each macro is one line: a colour, the row it controls, which channels of that row it reaches, how the movement is shared between them, and the amount. Add a macro uses one of the eight, and the cross at the end of the line frees it again.

**The eight macros are a pool, not a limit you are meant to notice.** A plugin declares its parameters once when it is created, and neither VST3 nor AU can add one later. So making a macro uses one of eight that already exist, and removing it frees it again. The panel shows the ones you have made, and your host's parameter list shows all eight whether you use them or not.

**Scope** is All, Odd, Even, or any one interval: choosing fifths reaches harmonics 3, 6, 12 and 24. **Curve** is Uniform or Taper. A taper has the most effect on a channel you pick, and less with distance on either side of it. Link's third curve, Spread, is not available and cannot be. It moves each strip in a direction based on your drag relative to the strip under the mouse, and a macro has no drag direction and no strip under the mouse.

**A macro offsets the patch's values instead of writing them.** Nothing in your sound is overwritten, the host has one lane to draw instead of thirty-two to record, and the knobs do not move when a macro does. That last part is normal for controls that work this way, but it can be surprising at first, so the controls show both values at once. The ring around a knob lights up to the value the macro has set, in the macro's colour, while the pointer on the cap stays at the patch's value, in the channel's colour. The gap between them is the macro. A fader has no ring, so it shows this in the gutters on either side of its track. Two narrow columns of segments appear there, in the same style as the meter behind the fader, and light from the bottom of the track up to the level the macro has set. The glass of the cap is tinted in the same colour.

With a macro at rest the two are in the same place, so a macro you have assigned but not moved looks the same as no macro.

On a [silenced channel](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/controls/#silenced) the macro's ring and columns go dark with the rest of the strip, and only the pointer and the fader cap still show the patch's value.

The amount runs from -1 to +1 whatever it controls, so a macro can always push a control either way from the patch's value. It moves each control by a proportion of its own range, not by a number of units. This matters most on a row like decay, which runs from a thousandth of a second to twenty seconds. Adding the same number of seconds would be a twentyfold change at one end and almost no change at the other.

A full sweep reaches the ends of the range, so if the patch value is already near one end, part of the macro's travel does nothing in that direction. This is on purpose. One macro reaches up to 32 controls that may be set anywhere, so no smaller part of the range would suit all of them.

**Right-click a macro's amount to bind a controller to it**, using the same MIDI Learn as the mixer's controls. Only the amount can be bound, because the row, the scope and the curve define the macro rather than move it. Its knob in the Playing bar has the same option, with Edit macro beside it to open MACROS. For a macro not yet made, the knob offers Assign macro instead, which creates the macro and opens MACROS. The macros icon lights whenever any macros exist, because otherwise you cannot see a macro's effect without looking at a ring.

## Playing it from a controller

**Right-click any control and choose MIDI Learn**, then move something on your controller. A violet ring marks the control while it waits, so you can see which control is listening without opening the menu again. Only one control can wait at a time. Right-click the same control afterwards and the menu shows which controller moves it, with options to remove the binding or bind a different one. In the mixer these items are below the LINK settings in the right-click menu. On the top bar, the Playing and Tuning bars and the noise channel, they have a menu of their own, because none of these is part of the series LINK gangs.

Your host almost certainly offers the same thing. The difference is that here you set up the mapping by right-clicking the knob itself, instead of finding `H17 AM Rate` in a list of 850 parameters, and it works the same way in every host.

**Eleven controllers cannot be bound**, because the instrument already uses them and losing them would affect your playing. Controller 1 is the mod wheel, which can drive aftertouch. 64 is the sustain pedal. 74 is the slide axis, the easiest to bind by accident because it moves whenever a finger moves on an MPE keyboard. 120 and 123 stop notes. Controllers 6, 38, 98, 99, 100 and 101 are how a keyboard tells the instrument what kind of keyboard it is. If you arm a knob and then touch the slide to steady a note, the note is steadied and the knob keeps waiting.

**It works the same with MPE on**, which takes extra handling. With MPE on, nearly every message goes to the part of the instrument that reads your keyboard's layout, so bindings are checked before that, not after. Otherwise MIDI Learn would not work on the controllers the instrument is most often played from.

The mapping is saved with your project, along with the window size and the folded sections, and **a preset never changes it**. Which controller moves which knob depends on your hardware setup, not on the sound, so a patch should not change it. A binding stores the parameter by name, so a later version that adds controls cannot quietly point it at something else.

Two things to expect. A control jumps to the controller's current position instead of waiting for the controller to reach it, so a hardware knob turned to the top takes the parameter there the moment you touch it. And undo does not reverse changes made from a controller, for the same reason it does not reverse automation.
