Page: Overtonium presets: the thirty-five that ship, and saving your own
URL: https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/presets/
Last changed: 2026-10-15

# Presets

Thirty-five presets ship with the plugin. All but a handful were set up on the panel and converted directly from the saved file. What ships is exactly what was played, not an approximation written afterwards.

## Hear them played

Eleven of them, played live, not rendered. The clips further down are one chord each, the same chord every time. That makes them easy to compare, but it does not show what a preset does when someone plays it. The video shows that.

Played on an Expressive E Osmose, with nothing on the output but the plugin's own effects.

[Video: Overtonium sound examples](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA)

Straight to one of them:

- [0:00 Synth Ensemble](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=0s)
- [2:04 Metallic Piano](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=124s)
- [2:55 Dream Phase](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=175s)
- [4:04 FM Piano](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=244s)
- [5:47 Sparkle Pad](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=347s)
- [6:56 Dire Dire EP](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=416s)
- [7:06 Music Box](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=426s)
- [7:25 Stepped](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=445s)
- [8:32 Wurli](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=512s)
- [8:45 Lo-fi](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=525s)
- [10:03 Nylon EP](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1oYdPxGlGA&t=603s)

## What ships

Thirty-five presets. Only two of them are versions of one patch, and they are the place to start: **Just Saw** and **Equal Saw** are identical except for [TUNE](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/), and they sound nothing alike.

Each clip plays the same thing: a spread C major chord, played a note at a time and released all at once. This makes it easy to listen through them in order. The clips are rendered by the plugin, not recorded, so they always match what it does. The levels are the ones each preset sets, not matched to each other. Nothing downloads until you press play.

Twenty-eight of them use one of the six [oscillator characters](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/effects/#character). The character is part of the patch like everything else here, so what you hear is the preset as it ships. Keep two of the six in mind while listening. Bulb is only audible when the pitch moves, and Op-amp only affects partials above a kilohertz. Both do more when you play them on a keyboard than in a clip of a held chord.

**2-bit Fuzz Organ**

An organ at 8 kHz and 2 bits, where the aliasing and the quantisation noise provide the distortion. The modulation wheel or aftertouch blends the root note towards a fifth

**60s Organ**

A worn combo organ, with a few milliseconds of key click on every note. It goes into a bucket brigade delay driven so hard that the repeats grow instead of fading, then into a spring reverb long enough to still ring when the next chord starts

**6581 Triangle**

The triangle wave of a MOS 6581, the SID chip in a Commodore 64. A triangle wave has odd harmonics that fall with the square of their number, and this is not quite that. The chip folds the top bit of its accumulator and drops the lowest one, so it draws a staircase instead of a straight line. That adds even harmonics and a noise floor under them, and these are most of what makes a SID sound like a SID

**Big Saw**

A sawtooth with a little randomness in it, so it drifts and beats instead of staying still

**Cathedral**

A principal chorus: octaves and fifths only, a registration an organ builder would recognise. It fades in slowly, the way pipes start to sound

**DigiLog**

A digital instrument played through worn analogue gear, at 16 kHz and 8 bits. The envelope delay gets longer for higher partials, so the series comes in from the bottom up. It opens in steps like a filter, not in a smooth sweep

**Dire Dire EP**

A soft, round electric piano of the kind used in underwater music. It is dark except for the 13th and 15th partials, which stand out from their neighbours as the tine

**Drawbar Organ**

Nine drawbars, with the key-off stage used as a release click. The upper drawbars jump to 55% for two milliseconds as the contacts break

**Dream Phase**

A strike that turns into a pad, without using separate layers. The short partials make the transient and the long ones come in behind them as it opens. Two partials step on square waves underneath, and the echo is nearly all feedback

**EP Chimes**

A round electric piano with bright chimes above it, at 16 kHz and 8 bits, so the artefacts are part of the sound and not added on top

**Equal Saw**

Just Saw with every partial moved to equal temperament

**FM Piano**

The electric piano sound of an FM synthesizer such as the DX7, not the instrument it imitates

**Glass Armonica**

Wet fingers on glass. Each partial arrives later and vibrates faster than the one below it

**Glide**

A pad that comes in from the bottom up. The fundamental starts at once and every partial above it glides in a little later. Played softly it is round and slow, and played hard it is bright and punchy

**Glockenspiel**

A struck bar. Nothing sustains, so every partial fades from the moment it is hit, each over its own length of time. The tone comes from the fourth and eleventh partials more than from the fundamental

**Init**

The neutral starting point: the first three partials and nothing else. It clears the patch and does not change the session settings

**Just Saw**

The same sound as Equal Saw with every partial at its exact whole-number ratio

**Lo-fi**

8 kHz and 8 bits, soft, with very short partials starting at different times. Close to the sound of a Roland D-50, a Korg Wavestation or a granular synthesizer

**Metallic Piano**

A thin, metallic upright piano. The [resonator](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/effects/#resonator) rings the strings of the keys you hold, and every string while the sustain pedal is down

**Music Box**

Plucked steel teeth, with irregular vibrato on each partial and one partial bent much further than the rest

**Nylon EP**

A very round electric piano, as if the tines were nylon instead of steel

**Odd Harmonics**

Every even partial is silent, which gives the hollow tone of a stopped pipe. Velocity opens the top of the series

**Omni-84**

The SonicStrings Voice 2 from a Suzuki Omnichord OM-84 System Two

**Shimmer**

Every partial rises and falls in level at its own rate, so the spectrum never repeats

**Slow Pad**

Staggered envelope delays, so the spectrum builds up gradually instead of starting at once, with mirrored pans across the series

**Space Cowboy**

A synthetic tremolo guitar, plucked from [the string in the noise channel](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/controls/#noise), over a pad with square-wave pitch modulation in some of its partials, and a whistle like a theremin that glides between overlapping notes. The [resonator](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/effects/#resonator) rings under all of it

**Space Flute**

A pan flute in the distance. The breath is on the noise channel, and the echo and the reverb give the distance

**Sparkle Pad**

Two instruments, split by where a partial sits in the series. The bottom three partials sustain and take up to three quarters of a second to come in. Everything above them starts at once and is gone within half a second

**Stepped**

A slow pad that keeps moving. Seven partials trill on square waves set to whole intervals, two at a fifth and five at an octave. The top three take their level from sample and hold

**Struck Bell**

Higher partials fade first, which is what makes something sound struck. Play harder and the upper partials come in

**StyloPoly**

Voice 3 of a Dubreq Stylophone S-1 with the vibrato on. Unlike the Stylophone it is polyphonic, but the vibrato is shared across the keyboard, as it is on the original with its single oscillator. Every partial's level moves on its own smooth random path

**Synth Ensemble**

Strings and brass in one patch. Nothing in it starts at the same moment, and how hard you play sets how far apart things start. A hard chord starts at once. A quiet one swells in over a couple of seconds, with the series drifting apart on the way

**Tape Choir**

Like a vowel: a formant peak in the low partials instead of a straight roll-off, and an old echo machine with dark, unsteady repeats

**Vibraphone**

A fast strike where the fundamental rings for seconds and everything above it is gone within one second

**Wurli**

A Wurlitzer 200A electric piano, with one tremolo circuit for the whole keyboard instead of one per tine, so a whole chord pulses together

## What a preset carries

The patch and nothing else. Everything in the Settings menu stays as you set it. This is a general rule, not a list that could get out of date: you set up the instrument in the menu and make the sound on the panel. So loading a preset never changes your polyphony, your temperament, your reference pitch, your pitch bend range, your MPE or aftertouch routing, or Adaptive's Retune, harmonic sevenths and No drift. It also leaves your window size and your [LINK](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/controls/#link) settings alone. These belong to the session you are working in, not to any one sound in it, and a patch that reset you to equal temperament in the middle of a piece would get in the way. The master fader and the output stage are different. They are on the panel and part of the sound, so a preset loads at the level it was made at, through the clipper it was made with.

Presets you save follow the same rule as the ones that ship, and store exactly the same set of controls. If a preset file contains any of these settings, it still loads, and those settings are ignored.

This includes Init. It is a preset too, so it clears the patch and leaves the session settings as you set them.

Values are stored as plain values, not normalised, so a preset still works if a parameter's range is widened later. Anything a file does not mention keeps its default value.

## Switching them over MIDI

A MIDI program change loads a factory preset, so a keyboard, a foot controller or a clip in your host can change the sound without anyone using the menu. The number selects the entry by its position in the Factory list, counting from zero. The list is alphabetical. Hosts and hardware that number program changes from one are one higher, so their 1 is the first entry. A number past the last preset is ignored. It does not wrap round to the start.

The preset is loaded even if it is the one already showing, as a program change does on a hardware instrument with a panel. So a clip that starts with a program change sounds the same every time it plays, and anything you changed by hand is replaced. If you want to keep those edits, save them as your own preset first.

Only the factory presets have numbers. Your own presets live in a folder you can add to and rename at any time, so their positions would not stay fixed long enough for a clip to rely on them. The same applies across versions. A release that adds a factory preset moves every preset that comes after it alphabetically, so a clip made with an older version can select a different sound in a newer one. Sessions are not affected, because a saved session stores the preset's name as well as its number, and the name is what is used.

Program changes work on any channel, MPE included, and load the same things as loading a preset by hand. Your polyphony, temperament and the rest of the Settings menu stay as you set them.

## Saving your own

Saving writes one small file per preset. The menu reads that folder every time it opens, so a preset added from outside the plugin shows up without a restart. The folder is created when it is first needed.

**The bar shows the loaded preset's name on a display of nine cells.** A longer name is shortened in steps, not just cut off. The spaces go first, then the vowels from the right, and only then is the rest trimmed. So *Tape Choir* keeps every letter as TAPECHOIR and *Glass Armonica* becomes GLASSRMNC. The menu, the file on disk and your host all get the full name. Saving does not change the name.

| Platform | Where they live |
|---|---|
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Dehli Musikk/Overtonium/Presets` |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\Dehli Musikk\Overtonium\Presets` |
| Linux | `~/.config/Dehli Musikk/Overtonium/Presets` |

They are small XML files of parameter values, so you can read them, edit them, keep them under version control and share them by copying the file. The menu sorts them by name, not in the order the filesystem returns them.

**Folders become groups.** Make a folder in the preset folder and it appears in the menu as a submenu with everything inside it, nested as deeply as you nest the folders. There is nothing to set up and nothing else to manage. The folders are the groups, so to move a preset between groups you move the file. Groups are listed before the presets that are not in a group, and the loaded preset has a tick wherever it is.

Page: Installing Overtonium on macOS, Windows and Linux
URL: https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/install/
Last changed: 2026-10-16

# Installing

Installers for macOS and Windows, and a zip for Linux. Every release also has a zip next to the installer with the same builds unpacked, for anyone without administrator rights or who keeps plugins in their own folders.

## Download

Five files. Most people want the installer for their platform.

| File | Holds | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| [macOS installer](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/download/v1.14.0/Overtonium-v1.14.0-macOS.pkg) | VST3, Audio Unit, Standalone | The usual choice on a Mac. You choose which of the three formats to install |
| [macOS zip](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/download/v1.14.0/Overtonium-v1.14.0-macOS.zip) | VST3, Audio Unit, Standalone | On a Mac without administrator rights, or if you keep your plugins in a folder of your own |
| [Windows installer](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/download/v1.14.0/Overtonium-v1.14.0-Windows.exe) | VST3, Standalone | The usual choice on Windows. It needs administrator rights, and SmartScreen will say the publisher is unknown |
| [Windows zip](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/download/v1.14.0/Overtonium-v1.14.0-Windows.zip) | VST3, Standalone | On Windows without administrator rights, if you keep your plugins in a folder of your own, or if you would rather not run an unsigned installer |
| [Linux zip](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/download/v1.14.0/Overtonium-v1.14.0-Linux.zip) | VST3, LV2, Standalone | The only download for Linux. There is no installer, because Linux distributions do not agree on where plugins go |

Every file above is from **version 1.14.0**, released 16 October 2026. [What changed in it](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/releases/), and in every version before it, has a page of its own. Older builds and the source are on the [releases page](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/latest).

## What each platform gets

| Platform | Installer | Formats |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | `.pkg`, with a chooser | VST3, Audio Unit, Standalone |
| Windows | `.exe` | VST3, Standalone |
| Linux | none, use the zip | VST3, LV2, Standalone |

### macOS

The package asks which of the three formats you want and installs only those. It is a universal binary, so one download covers Apple Silicon and Intel, and it is signed and notarised, so it opens without a warning. The minimum is macOS 10.13 on Intel and 11.0 on Apple Silicon, which is the lowest version the toolchain supports for that architecture.

### Windows

The installer is not signed, so SmartScreen says the publisher is unknown. Choose "More info" and then "Run anyway". If you would rather not, [build it from source](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/install/#building) instead. The VST3 goes to the shared plugin folder, so the installer asks for administrator rights.

### Linux

There is no installer, because Linux distributions do not agree on an install location. The zip holds VST3, LV2 and standalone, and the two plugin folders go in `~/.vst3` and `~/.lv2`.

## When a host does not see it

| Symptom | What to try |
|---|---|
| Logic or GarageBand shows no Overtonium | They only look for new Audio Units when they start. Quit and reopen instead of rescanning |
| A host lists it but will not load it | Check you have the right format. Logic uses the Audio Unit and most others use the VST3. It is easy to install only one of the two by accident in the chooser |
| Nothing appears after installing on macOS | Confirm where the files went with `pkgutil --files com.dehlimusikk.overtonium.vst3`. The plugins belong in `/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins` and the app in `/Applications` |
| The plugin loads but is silent | Check the master fader and whether a channel is [soloed](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/controls/). Solo is per channel and mute overrides solo, so a soloed strip can still be muted |
| Held notes sound but nothing new does | Overtonium is a synthesizer and needs MIDI. Check the track's input, not the plugin |

Please report anything else on the [issue tracker](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/issues), especially on Windows and Linux, for the reason below.

## Telling you about new versions

The check is off unless you turn it on. The first time you open the window, a dialog asks whether to turn it on. Nothing goes out to the network unless you say yes. Either answer is remembered, so you are not asked again. After that, the setting is under Settings.

With it on, the plugin downloads one small file from this site when the window opens and compares the version in it with the build you are running. If there is a newer version, a dialog says so, once for each release, SETTINGS lights up, and the first item in its menu opens the release page. It is a plain request for a static file: no identifier, no telemetry, nothing about your machine. The [security policy](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/blob/main/SECURITY.md) lists exactly what is sent.

The dialogs are drawn inside the plugin's own window, not opened as separate windows. A plugin cannot tell whether someone is opening it or a host is scanning its plugin folder at startup, and a window that waited for an answer would stop the scan. These dialogs do not wait for anything, and a question only counts as asked once someone has answered it.

## What it costs to run

Polyphony is what matters most, because eight voices of 32 partials is 256 sine oscillators. Measured on one core at 48 kHz with everything running at once: both modulators on every channel, drift, velocity, aftertouch, the meters and the noise channel.

| Voices | Oscillators | One core |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 32 | about 1% |
| 8, the default | 256 | about 7% |
| 16 | 512 | 14 to 15% |

The effects on the bar add to that, and cost the same at any polyphony, because they process the sum and not each voice. Most of them cost far less than the voices: the room and the plate are around half a percent each and the echoes less. The spring is the exception at about two and a half percent, because its dispersion is a chain of filters per spring and there are three springs. The resonator costs about a tenth of what eight voices do in Piano or Octave. In Open, or in Piano with the sustain pedal down, all eighty-eight of its strings are free to ring, and it costs about half of what eight voices do. These are one machine's figures and not a promise about yours, but the proportions hold: the voices are the main cost, and the resonator with all its strings free is the only effect that comes near them.

**The render rate is the control to reach for** if you need it cheaper. Turning it down really lowers the rate, it is not a filter on top. The whole voice pool renders at the lower rate, and at 8 kHz it costs a fifth as much. You can also hear it, which is why it is on the panel and not in a preferences dialog. Lowering the polyphony also works, in proportion.

What keeps it affordable is that the engine stays a plain bank of oscillators. It uses a 4096-point interpolated sine table instead of a sine call per sample. Modulators and envelope coefficients update once per 32-sample block, and only the oscillator and the envelope run at sample rate. A partial that is muted, faded out or at zero skips the oscillator entirely.

## What has been tested

All three platforms are built and run through the test suite on every push, and the VST3 is checked with pluginval at strictness 8 on each of them. macOS is the only platform where the plugin has been loaded into a real host, and there the Audio Unit and the VST3 also pass `auval`. Nobody has run the Windows or Linux builds in a DAW yet, so treat those as untested.

## Building from source

You need CMake 3.22 or newer and a C++17 compiler. JUCE is downloaded at configure time, so there is nothing else to install on macOS or Windows.

```
git clone https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium.git
cd overtonium
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
```

The plugins are copied into your user plugin folders as part of the build. Pass `-DOVERTONIUM_INSTALL_AFTER_BUILD=OFF` to skip that. Linux needs a handful of development packages first, which the [contributing guide](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#linux) lists.

The build treats warnings as errors, the same as the project's own checks. If your compiler is one the project has not been tested with, add `-DOVERTONIUM_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=OFF` to the first cmake command and it builds anyway.

Overtonium is free software under the AGPLv3, which follows from JUCE. The whole source, including the tests and the packaging, is in the [repository](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium).

---

Page: Overtonium releases: what changed in each version
URL: https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/releases/
Last changed: 2026-10-16

# Releases

What changed in each version, newest first. Each one links to its full notes, which say more and carry the installing and upgrading detail as well.

## 1.14.0, 16 October 2026

**A string in the noise channel.** A Karplus-Strong string the noise strikes, tuned to the note and following the wheel, glide, MPE and every temperament. STRING, DECAY, DAMP and POINT sit under COLOUR. A short noise envelope plucks it and a held one blows into it, so a pluck and a pitched breath are settings, not modes.

**The resonator.** Eighty-eight sympathetic strings that ring with what you play, before the bus drive, in their own frame on the top bar. Piano frees the strings of held keys and the sustain pedal frees the rest, Open keeps the pedal down, Octave rings twelve strings from C3 and Series the root's own harmonics. MIX, DECAY and DAMP keep the level about the same across their range. The new preset Space Cowboy uses both, and Metallic Piano now rings its own strings.

**A rearranged top bar and a faster mixer.** The four buttons come first, then the wordmark over the preset screen, with the spacing evened out. The update question is asked inside the window, and SETTINGS stays lit while a new version waits. Silenced channels and switched-off stages turn their lights fully off. Soloing, scrolling and resizing redraw the mixer far faster. A wheel over a knob in the bars no longer scrolls the mixer, Fit all 32 channels gives every row its full height, and JUCE 9.0.4 fixes a possible crash in Windows hosts when a window closes.

**Before upgrading.** Space Cowboy sorts at program 25, so a MIDI program change from 25 up lands one preset later, while a saved session keeps its preset by name. Metallic Piano sounds fuller than it did. There are 850 parameters, the eight new ones on the end.

[The full notes for 1.14.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.14.0)

## 1.13.0, 13 October 2026

**Adaptive, a temperament that retunes as you play.** After Eivind Groven's organs, every pitch class has five versions a comma apart, and the chord you hold is kept on whichever make it purest, settled again every time a key goes down or comes up. A held note the next chord needs elsewhere slides there over the Retune time. A dominant seventh is tuned on the harmonic seventh, 4:5:6:7, and NO DRIFT keeps the keyboard home where a progression would carry it off a comma at a time. Every one of the 125 chord types in music-utils is played through it in all twelve keys on every build.

**Two bars under the top bar.** PLAYING and TUNING open a bar each, both closed until you open them. The Tuning bar shows twelve displays, one for each note, saying how far it sits from equal temperament in cents, in every temperament, and under Adaptive a PURE lamp, 7:4, DRIFT, NO DRIFT and the Retune knob. The Playing bar holds the voice and expression settings, shows the voices in use, the sustain pedal, the pitch wheel, the mod wheel and pressure, and carries the eight macros as knobs captioned with what they are aimed at, which a right-click assigns, opens in MACROS or binds to a controller.

**Displays that behave like real ones, and No stack.** Every segment display is a fixed row of cells that light or stay dark, with no dimmed figures, cleaner letters and a proper sharp sign. One voice per key is renamed No stack, for what it does. Right-clicking a knob on the top bar now offers MIDI Learn, which it never did.

**Before upgrading.** Adaptive is a seventh entry on the temperament list, so temperament automation drawn against six lands a little further along, while a saved session keeps its temperament. A host shows No Stack, Pitch Mod Shared and Amp Mod Shared in place of the old names, with the same ids. There are 842 parameters.

[The full notes for 1.13.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.13.0)

## 1.12.0, 10 October 2026

**Glide on every channel.** Every channel has its own glide time, the last row under PITCH MOD, from Off to five seconds. Because each partial travels on its own time, the series does not have to arrive together: short times on the top land the brightness first and let the pitch follow, and the other way round the note arrives and its colour catches up. The needle on each partial's PITCH MOD rule follows the glide back to centre. Two switches govern every channel at once, as lit letters beside the GLIDE caption: **L** glides always or only legato, and **T** makes the time a fixed rate per octave or a fixed time however far a note goes.

**ATTACK reaches into where a partial starts.** The PHASE knob is gone. Turned past its shortest time, ATTACK reads in degrees, from a rising zero crossing at 0° to the partial's own peak at 90°, and STRIKE moves along the whole knob, so a hard blow lands on the peak and a light one travels up into a short attack.

**Legato is a switch, and with more than one voice it plays a top line.** With one voice it is the monophonic legato it always was. With more, a melody held from note to note carries on over chords that still retrigger each time their keys come up and go down, and the note a melody carries on from always sounds. A wrong guess about which key is the melody costs an attack and nothing more.

**Shared by all notes, a thirty-fourth preset, and a quieter panel.** The in-phase switch is renamed for what it does and has a switch of its own beside each SHAPE caption. *Glide* is a pad whose partials glide in up the series, round played softly and bright played hard. The panel is a shade darker with lighter captions, which now clear the 4.5:1 contrast the accessibility standard asks for, and a dark sliver at the top left corner of every screen and lamp is gone.

**Before upgrading.** The Limiter's lookahead is off by default, so new instances report 12 samples of latency at 48 kHz rather than 108, and a saved session keeps its setting. Start phase is gone, so a patch that set one starts each partial at the zero crossing, and an automation lane on it in a host that goes by position now moves glide. ATTACK automation drawn against the old travel lands on different times. *Glide* sorts after *Glass Armonica*, so a MIDI program change will name the preset above the one it used to, while a saved session carries the name and is unaffected. There are 839 parameters.

[The full notes for 1.12.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.12.0)

## 1.11.1, 7 October 2026

**Four controls read to seven decimal places.** The pitch modulator's rate and depth, the drift and the amplitude modulator's rate had no text of their own, so a host's automation lane, the panel's value popup and a screen reader all said `4.0000005 Hz` for four. They now read as the other controls do, `4.00 Hz`, `30.0 Hz` and `0 ct`. The macro amount reads as the panel shows it, `-100.0 %` to `+100.0 %`, rather than to four places, and a value typed into a host is read as a percentage. Only the text changed: ranges, defaults and stored values are as they were, so sessions, presets and automation play back exactly as before.

[The full notes for 1.11.1](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.11.1)

## 1.11.0, 7 October 2026

**Eight macros, so a relationship across the series can be automated.** A LINK drag moves 32 parameters and a host catches only the last one touched, so a relationship you can edit by hand could not be recorded at all. A macro names a row, a scope and a curve, and gives that relationship one control and the host one lane. It offsets rather than writes, so the patch underneath is untouched, which is why the knobs do not move when a macro does. A driven control says both things at once instead: the ring of ticks lights to where the macro has taken the value in the macro's colour, and the pointer stays at what the patch holds. A fader says it in the gutters either side of its track. Eight is a pool rather than a count, since a plugin declares its parameters once and cannot add one later.

**MIDI Learn.** Right-click a control, choose MIDI Learn, move something on the controller. One parameter per controller number, saved with the session rather than with a patch, because which controller moves which knob describes the desk rather than the sound. Eleven numbers are refused rather than bound, the mod wheel and the MPE slide among them, so arming a knob and then reaching for the slide to steady a note leaves the note steadied and the knob still waiting.

**CLIP is five machines instead of a switch.** *Soft* is the curve that was already there and came through bit for bit. *Hard* is a wall at unity. *Asymmetric* lets one half of the wave lean over first, the way a single-ended stage runs out of supply in one direction, which gives even harmonics where the others give odd. *Limiter* does not bend the wave at all, it moves the level. *Fold* turns the wave back on itself and sings where the rest crunch. All five are bounded by full scale, tested at drives up to 400 times at three sample rates. The limiter looks ahead two milliseconds, which is what took the reported latency from 12 samples to 108 at 48 kHz, and Settings can refuse it.

**The parameters scroll.** The rows are small on a 1080p screen and zooming in to read them made the window taller than such a screen has room for. A channel is three bands now: the channel number at the top and the fader at the foot are pinned, and everything between them scrolls behind an opening, so neither of the two things you find your place by is ever what has scrolled away.

**The panel was rebuilt.** Every switch is a lit plastic cap in a moulded well, with a fixed near-black legend printed on the plastic so a word does not change colour under its own lamp. The knobs are discs with an eight-slot collar, and the notches are cut out of it rather than painted on. The preset name is spelled on a fourteen-bar display. The OUTPUT rule carries two lamps, VELOCITY on the left and AFTERTOUCH on the right, so all five rules say something. LINK and DRAW became one tool button rather than two switches that could not both be on, and choosing a scope now lights the channel number of every strip a drag would reach.

**A thirty-third preset, and an accessibility statement.** *6581 Triangle* is the triangle of a MOS 6581, the SID in a Commodore 64, which is not quite a triangle: the chip draws its ramp as a staircase of 2048 steps, so it carries even harmonics a triangle should not have. `ACCESSIBILITY.md` says what is checked rather than intended, and says plainly that the plugin's own window is not keyboard operable and that nobody who relies on assistive technology has evaluated any of it.

**Fixed.** A partial silenced by a negative AFTERTOUCH amount took every lamp on its channel dark with it, which had been wrong for the envelope and tremolo lamps since those lamps existed. And a note played while the channel was already under pressure thumped or faded in, because the pressure smoother started from nothing at every note-on instead of from where the channel was holding it.

**Before upgrading.** The plugin reports 108 samples of latency at 48 kHz where it reported 12, which is the limiter's window, and Settings can take it back. Loading a preset now moves the master fader and the clipper, since both left the settings a preset cannot reach. *6581 Triangle* sorts third, so a MIDI program change will name the preset above the one it used to, while a saved session carries the name as well as the number and is unaffected. Fifty parameters were added, 836 in all, all of them on the end, so every automation lane written before this release still points at the control it was pointing at.

[The full notes for 1.11.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.11.0)

## 1.10.1, 30 September 2026

**Removing the plugin could hang the host.** In a host that unloads the plugin binary once no instances are left, taking the last one out could lock the host up, with no way out but to end the process. Reported in FL Studio and in Reaper, while hosts that keep the binary loaded were never affected.

The texture the panels are drawn with is an image, built the first time a window opens and shared by every window after it, and it was being kept for the life of the process. Under Windows that image lives on the graphics card, so letting go of it hands resources back to the driver, and keeping it in a static meant that happened while the host was unloading the binary. Windows holds a lock for the whole of an unload and the driver work cannot run until that lock is free, so neither finishes. The texture now belongs to the windows that use it and goes when the last one closes. Nothing else changed, and nothing about the sound has.

## 1.10.0, 30 September 2026

**The echo is three machines, and so is the reverb.** Both were a switch that turned one thing on, and both are now a button that says which machine is running. *Tape* is the loop that was already there. *BBD* is a line of buckets, which gets darker the longer you set it to, because a longer delay can only be had by clocking the buckets more slowly and the filter has to come down with the clock. *Digital* does not pretend to be anything and is the only ping-pong of the three, crossing every repeat to the other side where the other two never cross at all. AGE is the same knob on all three and asks each for the thing that machine gets worse at: tape wear, a slowing clock and a breathing compander, or falling bits and sample rate.

*Room* is the reverb that was already there. *Modulated plate* is a sheet of steel with no geometry to hear, so a hit spreads across all of it at once and the tail is dense from its first instant rather than arriving in stages. It is called modulated because it is: its allpasses wander six times as far as the shape they come from gives them, and without that a long decay repeats its own pattern instead of washing. *Spring* is a tray of three helical springs, and a helix carries the top of the band faster than the bottom, so a hit comes back as a chirp that starts high and falls and every bounce adds another. DECAY, DAMP and PRE mean the same thing on all three, and the wet levels are matched, so switching machines changes the character of a tail rather than its length or its loudness.

**The character now says how hard the mix is driven.** The thirty-three channels are summed onto a bus that drives, by an amount belonging to the oscillator character. It answers to level rather than to a setting, which is what a table baked into one partial's waveform cannot do: play quietly and it is barely there, lean on the keyboard and it arrives. Bulb asks for the most and Diode the least, Pure sums cleanly and does nothing, and there is no knob, because how hard a summing amplifier is driven is part of what choosing a character means.

**How fast you let a key go sets the level its tail starts from.** On a keyboard that senses a release, the hardest lift doubles the key-off level and the softest halves it. There is no knob and no parameter: it is a property of the gesture the way velocity is, and a keyboard that cannot sense a release changes nothing.

**The master volume is a glass fader lying across the output meter**, over the lamps it sets the level of, instead of a knob in a group of its own. A LINK drag that spreads a move uniformly now spreads it in decibels as well: on the fader row it was uniform in travel, which put six or seven decibels on the loudest channel and thirty on the quietest.

**A thirty-second factory preset, and four others that reach for the new machines.** *60s Organ* is a combo organ that has not been serviced: the partials are pulled off each other rather than tuned, so the stack beats against itself instead of fusing, and the noise channel is a few milliseconds of key click on every note. It runs into a bucket brigade driven hard enough that the repeats grow rather than fade, and falls into a spring still ringing when the next chord arrives. It is also the first patch to ask for Diode. *Shimmer* and *Tape Choir* now ask for the plate rather than the room, and *Cathedral* and *Struck Bell* stay on the room. Because the list is alphabetical and 60s Organ sorts second, a MIDI program change now names the preset above the one it used to. A saved session is unaffected, since it carries the name as well as the number.

**LINK came back switched off.** Its scope and its curve were remembered with the session and the switch that decides whether either applies was not, so reopening a window gave you exactly the drag you had set up, turned off. All three are saved together now.

**Unfolding a section made the faders swell.** On a window shrunk until the faders were squeezed, unfolding gave back twice the height it had taken, all of it to the faders. Applying the window's new size limits is itself a resize, so the height was measured after it had already moved and the same rows counted twice.

**Draw the faders.** A drag across the fader area sets every channel it passes over from the pointer's height, so a spectrum goes in with one stroke instead of thirty-two drags. Hold shift for it, or latch it on with the new DRAW switch under the LEVEL caption. Armed, every fader lights in the same accent the switch does, so what a drag would reach is visible before you touch anything. It is not LINK under another name: LINK shares one relative move out across the channels by a rule, and this sets absolute values freehand. Columns crossed between one moment and the next are filled in, the whole stroke is one undo, and the noise channel draws with the rest. While it is armed the pointer becomes a pencil and LINK reads as off, without being off.

**A section folds from any strip, not just from the gutter.** Every section draws a rule across all thirty-three columns, lined up with its heading in the caption gutter on the far left, and clicking one of those rules now folds that section. Reaching the gutter meant leaving the partial you were working on, crossing the mixer and finding your way back, by which time you had lost which column you were in. The pointer shows the same hand over a rule as over a heading.

**The bar says what each group is.** A small caption under the button at the head of the character, echo and reverb groups, because those buttons show a value and nothing said what OP-AMP, TAPE or ROOM was a choice of. With the caption doing that, the button reads OFF when the effect is off, where it used to read ECHO or REVERB so the group could still be found, and the ring of lit ticks around that effect's four knobs goes dark with it. The knobs keep their positions, so a setting can be dialled in before the thing is switched on. The clipper also has a switch on the bar now, CLIP, under the output meter beside the two converter readouts, which are a little larger themselves. It is still in the Settings menu too.

**Fixed.** Right-clicking the gap between two sections opened two LINK menus stacked on each other, and picking an item on the front one left the one behind it unchanged, so the setting looked to have been refused when it had already taken. A scroll over a knob also dragged the mixer sideways whenever the window was narrow enough for the series to need scrolling, since each strip watches everything inside it and passed the wheel on after the knob had taken it. A scroll on a strip's background still moves the series. The plugin would not tell you which version it was: not in the Settings menu, not on the panel, not anywhere, while the bug report template refused a report without one and said to read it off that menu. It is the menu's first heading now. The first repeat of an echo came back clean while every repeat after it was worn, on both the tape and the bucket brigade. Both echoes compressed everything they were handed, because the tape's backstop was set for a bus running near one where a full patch runs closer to two. The digital delay had a tail that never went away at any feedback from a half upwards, which is what a quantiser inside a feedback loop does. And the zoom menu ticked 100% whatever the zoom was.

**Before upgrading.** Presets on a character sound fuller, because the bus they are summed onto now drives, and that is the intended sound of them. The echoes are cleaner and their first repeat is coloured, so a patch leaning on the tape echo's compression will not find it. *Sparkle Pad* is louder and otherwise unchanged, since it was mixed low on purpose to keep that compression down. Your own patches get the tape and the room, which is what every patch written before this had. Two parameters were added, 786 in all, both on the end, so every automation lane written before this release still points at the control it was pointing at.

[The full notes for 1.10.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.10.0)

## 1.9.0, 23 September 2026

**Which oscillator the partials are.** A new control at the head of the series group, offering six of them. All six are sine oscillators, and what differs is the way each circuit fails to make one. *Pure* is the sine every partial already was. *Bulb* is a Wien bridge whose lamp lags, so the level sags behind every move of the pitch and recovers over about half a second. *Rail* grows into its own supply, *Diode* is bent into shape by two of them that do not match, and *Valve* is a triode with an octave on top of every partial. *Op-amp* is an amplifier that cannot keep up, so the top of the series hardens as it climbs while the bottom stays where it was. Each one is also a rack of thirty-two rather than one oscillator used thirty-two times: a fixed spread of a couple of cents and a fraction of a decibel, the same every time you load the patch. It is part of the patch, so a preset carries it, and twenty-five of the thirty-one factory presets now ask for one: eleven on Bulb, eight on Op-amp, four on Valve and two on Rail. Loading one of those gives what it ships as rather than what it was in 1.8.0, and setting the character back to Pure gives the older sound, except on *Synth Ensemble*, which was reworked further: its velocity amounts now take more of the series, so a soft chord arrives with less above the first few partials, and its reverb sits a third in rather than a quarter. A session is unaffected either way, since it carries the values rather than the preset's name.

**A MIDI program change loads a factory preset**, by its position in the alphabetical Factory list counting from zero, so a keyboard, a foot controller or a clip can change the sound without anyone touching the menu. A number past the last preset is ignored rather than wrapping.

**The converter readouts say what they are counting**, reading `48.0 kHz` and `8 bit` where they used to have room for the figure alone. LINK moved to the top of the caption column on the left to make that room, over the rows it gangs, and with it gone the bar fits on one row at the width the window opens at. Every switch on the panel now lights its word rather than its face, every screen and lamp is set into it with the lip of the opening it sits in, the standalone wears the instrument's own title bar instead of the grey-green one every unstyled JUCE application gets, and Settings has an entry that puts a window dragged narrow back to the width that shows all 32 channels.

**A modulator can be one circuit the whole keyboard hears.** Both belong to the note by default, so a chord struck a note at a time gives you three tremolos breathing out of step. The new entry at the foot of a shape button's menu, one for each modulator, hands the phase to the channel instead, so a note arriving late joins what is already running and a chord breathes as one thing. *Wurli* ships sharing its tremolo and *StyloPoly* its vibrato.

**Undo took a step several times a second while you were still turning a knob**, which was most obvious with a scroll wheel. A gesture is one step now, however many values it moved and however long it went on, and a gesture that ends where it began is not a step at all. A host playing an automation lane used to fill the history as well, and no longer leaves any: the history holds what a person did.

**Before upgrading.** Nothing you have made moves: a session opens sounding as it did, and your own presets get Pure and a modulator per note, which is what every patch written before this had. Twenty-five of the factory presets do sound different, since they now ask for a character, and two of those share a modulator across the keyboard as well. Three parameters were added, 784 in all, all three on the end, so every automation lane written before this release still points at the control it was pointing at.

[The full notes for 1.9.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.9.0)

## 1.8.0, 19 September 2026

**Three more factory presets, thirty-one in all.** All three lean on STRIKE, which arrived in 1.7.0 and is what lets one patch play two ways depending on how it is struck. *Glockenspiel* is a struck bar whose tone sits in the fourth and eleventh partials rather than the fundamental, with nothing sustaining and every partial ringing down for its own length. *Dream Phase* is a strike that becomes a pad, the short partials the transient and the long ones arriving behind them. *Sparkle Pad* splits the series in two: the bottom three sustain and arrive slowly, everything above attacks at once and is gone inside half a second.

**A session could open with the wrong preset showing as selected.** Presets sort alphabetically, so adding one moved every preset after it and an index saved last year named a different sound. The sound was never in doubt, since a session stores its values, but a host's program menu would highlight a patch the session was not playing. The saved name decides now, so reordering presets can no longer move a session onto a different one.

**Built on JUCE 9.0.2**, up from 8.0.15, with nothing in Overtonium needing to change for it. Every audio example on this site renders to the same samples before and after. Building from source on Linux now also needs `libxi-dev` and `libegl-dev`.

**Before upgrading.** The factory presets are renumbered, since the three new ones sort into alphabetical place. The sound is stored with the session either way, and with the fix above the name you saved is what the menu goes by. No parameter was added or removed, so automation is unaffected.

[The full notes for 1.8.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.8.0)

## 1.7.0, 12 September 2026

**STRIKE aims key velocity at the front of the envelope.** It sits at the head of the ENVELOPE group on every one of the thirty-three channels, above DELAY and ATTACK, because it is about the blow rather than about the shape. A hard note starts sooner and arrives faster, a soft one waits and then opens slowly. Each knob below it stays the limit of its own row: velocity only ever lengthens the attack and only ever pulls the delay in, so ATTACK goes on meaning the fastest that partial gets and DELAY the latest it ever arrives. The range is wide because the attacks worth stretching are short, so 2 ms under a hard blow is half a second under the softest. *Synth Ensemble* is rebuilt around it.

**MPE slide no longer lurches** on a controller whose slide axis rests at one end rather than at the centre. It is read as movement now: the first value a note is given becomes that note's nought, and what reaches the sound is how far the axis has travelled from it since. A Seaboard behaves as it always did. An Expressive E Osmose, which spends the first part of the key travel on pressure and only then starts sending slide, no longer jumps darker the instant the axis engages.

**Before upgrading.** LIFT is gone. It aimed release velocity at the key-off level and was the one control here that most keyboards cannot play, so a patch that used it loses those values and an automation lane pointed at one finds nothing. The parameter count is unchanged at 781 and everything else is untouched: every factory preset but *Synth Ensemble* renders to a byte-identical file before and after. A finger landing forward on a pad no longer starts the note bright, which is what reading slide as movement costs.

[The full notes for 1.7.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.7.0)

## 1.6.1, 11 September 2026

One fix, and nothing else. The waveform selectors added in 1.6.0 kept listening to their parameter fractionally longer than they should have, into the moment they were being taken apart, so a value arriving at exactly that instant landed on a control that was already half gone. Closing a plugin window while automation plays is the everyday version of that, which is why it was worth a release of its own rather than waiting.

[The full notes for 1.6.1](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.6.1)

## 1.6.0, 10 September 2026

**Both modulators pick a waveform.** Eight shapes on pitch and seven on amplitude, on every one of the thirty-three channels, so the fifth partial can be gated while the fourth breathes. The pitch depth reaches an octave now, which is what the shapes that step rather than sweep are worth having: a square on the pitch is a trill and sample and hold is a run of random notes. The tuning digits and the shape glyph are lit, so a strip has two displays rather than a screen and a label.

Two more factory presets, *Stepped* and *StyloPoly*, twenty-eight in all. Loading a preset used to tell the host about a thousand parameter changes, most of which were not changes, and now tells it only what moved.

**Before upgrading.** The factory presets are renumbered, since the two new ones sort into alphabetical place rather than onto the end, so a session that stored a preset by number opens on a different one. The sound is stored with the session either way. Automation is unaffected: the 65 new parameters are inserted among the existing ones, and both formats identify a parameter by name rather than by position.

[The full notes for 1.6.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.6.0)

## 1.5.0, 5 September 2026

Seven more factory presets, twenty-six in all, six of them the same electric piano seen from different angles, because that is what a stack of sine waves is good at. The preset menu became two submenus rather than one long list, and folders in your preset folder became groups in the menu.

**Nothing in the Settings menu travels with a preset any more.** Saving one used to write your polyphony, temperament, bend range and MPE into the file, so recalling a sound reached over and changed how the instrument was set up. The factory presets already knew better, and both kinds follow the same rule now.

Four fixes, the audible one being a note held by the sustain pedal clicking when you played it again. Its envelope restarted from silence while the note was still ringing at its sustain level.

[The full notes for 1.5.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.5.0)

## 1.4.0, 30 August 2026

Three more factory presets, nineteen in all. **Legato** arrived at the head of the polyphony list, where pressing a key while another is held moves the note rather than starting it again. **One voice per key** became a switch, so a bell struck over and over can be made to build up rather than take over its own voice. Right-clicking a mute or a solo clears every one of them across the mixer, which beats hunting for a stray solo among sixty-six buttons four pixels apart.

**Before upgrading.** Both lists gained an entry at the top, so polyphony indices shifted by one and a session saved on 8 voices opens on 6. The factory presets are renumbered for the same reason.

[The full notes for 1.4.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.4.0)

## 1.3.0, 28 August 2026

**The per-channel outputs are gone again**, and the release is mostly that removal. Logic offers a fixed menu of multi-output arrangements and cannot complete the larger ones, which arrangements work varies with the version and the processor underneath it, and the one shape that would actually suit a 32-partial mixer, 32 mono outputs, was never on the menu at all. A convenience that half worked in the one host it had been tried in is not part of the instrument.

Also fixed: parameters hold the values they are given. Two conversions between a knob position and a value were done in single precision, and 66 defaults fell where that round trip loses a bit.

[The full notes for 1.3.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.3.0)

## 1.2.0, 26 August 2026

An output per channel, 33 of them alongside the stereo mix, which 1.3.0 then removed. MPE slide gained a destination, off, brightness or tuning. The two LINK tilts became one **taper from wherever you grab**, which can peak under your hand in the middle of the series rather than only at an end. The level readout counts down to -99.9 dB rather than giving up at -66, which was two thirds of the fader's usable bottom end. Every control got a name a screen reader can read, all 635 of them.

**Before upgrading.** Automation written against the old level fader plays back at different levels, because the fader's travel is spaced by decibels now rather than by gain.

[The full notes for 1.2.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.2.0)

## 1.1.0, 24 August 2026

**Folding the mixer down.** Click a section heading in the caption gutter and that group of rows folds away across every channel at once, taking the window's height with it. All five groups is 480 pixels shorter.

The factory presets appeared in Logic's own preset menu, the panel gained its grain, its grooves and its bloom, and the [update check](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/install/) arrived, off unless you ask for it. Nothing about the sound changed, and a patch saved in 1.0.0 loads identically.

[The full notes for 1.1.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.1.0)

## 1.0.0, 23 August 2026

The first release. 32 sine partials and a noise channel, each with its own fader, tuning, envelope, tremolo, pitch modulation and pan. [TUNE](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/tuning/), six keyboard temperaments, inharmonic stretch, keyboard tracking, drift and wobble. MPE alongside ordinary MIDI, a tape echo, a feedback delay network reverb, a lo-fi converter, channel ganging, and 16 factory presets.

[The full notes for 1.0.0](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases/tag/v1.0.0)

## Being told about a new one

The plugin can check for itself, and does not unless you ask it to. The [install page](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/install/) says what that costs, which is one request for a static file and nothing about you. Every release is also on the [releases page](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases), which GitHub publishes as [a feed](https://github.com/benjamindehli/overtonium/releases.atom) for anyone who would rather subscribe than be asked.
